newsitem.title: VIETNAM: World's car makers play waiting game in Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: World's car makers play waiting game in Vietnam.

text.p: Vietnam's annual motorshow opened in a flourish of corporate razzmatazz on Thursday, but from behind their smart exhibition stands many car industry executives grumbled.
A brass band played and scantily-clad models pranced around shiny state-of-the-art cars as Vice-Minister for Industry Nguyen Xuan Chuan walked about, admiring the exhibits.
But, in a country where demand for new cars is barely 10,000 units a year, few at Auto Vietnam '96 pretended that Vietnam's market was a bonanza.
Ho Chi Minh City, the exhibition's venue, may be the commercial hub of one of the world's fastest growing economies, but here the roads swarm with bicycles and motorbikes, not cars.
"Anyone who's thinking about making and selling cars in Vietnam better be prepared for a long wait, because that's what it's going to be," said one European businessman at the show.
The government has granted licences to some 13 joint ventures to produce cars in Vietnam, a number many in the industry say has left too many scrambling for slices of a tiny market.
Among them is U.S. giant Ford Motor Company Its venture with Song Cong Diesel is on track to roll out its first vehicle, a Transit van, from a new $102 million plant near Hanoi in October 1997.

"I'm sure it's not going to be a cakewalk for the Ford Motor Company, we do have competitors," Ford's executive vice president Wayne Booker told a news conference. "But I have faith that the Vietnam economy will continue to grow."
While Ford said it intends to be a major player in Vietnam's car market, others have their doubts.
Chrysler Corp, for example, said it is reviewing plans to open a $192 million assembly plant near Ho Chi Minh City.
Vice-minister Chuan said in a magazine interview last weekend that demand for cars would accelerate rapidly in the years ahead, topping 80,000 by the turn of the century and 120,000 by 2005.
Automakers say that even if his upbeat forecasts are right, several major impediments remain to doing business in Vietnam.
These include huge taxes on car imports and quotas for imports of unassembled vehicles, known as complete knockdown kits (CKDs).
This year's CKD import quota is 6,000, a tiny number which has to be shared between the half-dozen plants now operating with an estimated combined capacity of close to 100,000 vehicles a year.
Marques currently produced in Vietnam include South Korea's Kia, Daimler-Benz Mercedes of Germany, Japan's Mitsubishi Motors and Nissan Motor Co.
Producers complain, however, that plants are standing largely idle for much of the year because of the current situation.

"The most troublesome problem now for the car assembling joint ventures in Vietnam is the quotas," Chuan conceded, adding that his ministry had proposed revising the quota system for importing spare parts.
Whether the quota system is relaxed or not, it is clear that the government wants to ensure that licensed car manufacturers produce a share of their components locally.
The companies are obliged to reach the rate of five percent of localised products in the first five years of operation and 30 percent after 10 years.
"That's going to be tough," said one Asian car company executive. "It would mean parts manufacturers setting up in Vietnam, and I just don't see them racing to do it."
